newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Suu Kyi urges UN rights body to denounce Burma.
newsitem.headline: Suu Kyi urges UN rights body to denounce Burma.

text.p: Burmese democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi, in a video message to the U.N. Human Rights Commission, appealed on Tuesday to the forum to adopt a strong resolution denouncing "repression" by the military regime.

In her taped remarks, Suu Kyi accused the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) of intimidating members of her National League for Democracy (NLD) party. Some had been forced to resign due to pressure on their families, she added.
She also said the government made civilians perform forced labour and relocate, causing ill health and death in some cases.

Suu Kyi, who won the 1991 Nobel Peace Prize for her non- violent efforts towards democracy, expressed concern that Karens along the Thai border and other ethnic nationalities were being subjected to "a lot of persecution, repression, forced porterage, torture and I am told even summary executions".
She urged the 53 members of the main U.N. human rights body, holding their annual six-week session in Geneva until April 18, to adopt a "strong resolution" condemning Rangoon.

"There are hardly any human rights which have not been violated by this military regime. And we need strong action from the international community to put an end to these constant violations of our basic human rights," she said.

Suu Kyi, speaking in the video, played on the sidelines of the Commission to a meeting of non-governmental organisations, added: "Restricting the NLD is tantamount to crushing democracy. Our political rights are getting fewer and fewer by the day.
"There are more restrictions, more repression. The authorities seem determined to crush any kind of political movement."
Burma is marshalling its allies to try to avert a repeat of the Commission adopting a resolution expressing its grave concern at "extremely serious" human rights violations in the country.

A letter signed by Ambassador U Aye on March 21 and sent to states which co-sponsored the resolution last April, argues that such resolutions are "extremely discriminatory, unbalanced and intrusive", according to a copy obtained by Reuters.

"...since the elements contained in the previous resolutions on Myanmar are detrimental to the cause you endorse, I am of the view that it would be beneficial for all if your country were to refrain from being a co-sponsor again should another draft resolution on Myanmar be tabled..." the letter adds.
Diplomats expect a draft resolution on Burma to be formally presented by Thursday, with voting scheduled for next Tuesday.

The U.N. rights investigator on Burma, in a report to the Commission issued last month, acccused its military government of arbitrary killings and torture mainly in the context of forced relocations and counter-insurgency operations in ethnic minority regions.

The U.N. report, by Mauritian laywer Rajsmoor Lallah, also said that Burma's "autocratic" power structure resulted in denial of fundamental civil and political rights, and that many political leaders remained in detention.
